ICO has issued a reprimand to West Midlands Police after the force repeatedly mixed up two data subject's personal information, violating several articles of the UK Data Protection Act.

The DPA ordered Google to deindex some URLs relating to data subject's non-payment of employee salary and insurance. The DPA postponed the decision for 7 more URLs until the data subject presents the required additional evidence and court decisions.

A data subject complained that Google LLC had refused to delist search results linked to his name, which concerned old press reports and alleged criminal offences. Google had delisted some links but kept others, arguing that the content related to his public business role and was accurate and current. The Authority held that six of the links were outdated (2008, 2011 and 2012 reports) or already removed at source, and ordered Google LLC to delist them from name-based search results. It rejected the request concerning the Blogger posts, since Google LLC was not the controller of that content.
The DPA fined a website provider €90,000 for setting unnecessary cookies without users’ consent and for not informing them about the existence and function of these cookies.

An Austrian resident, represented by noyb, complained that the Cyprus News Agency's website embedded Google Analytics, so that his IP address and cookie data may have reached Google LLC in the USA after the Schrems II judgment. The Commissioner found that the controller had not demonstrated compliance with the accountability principle (Art. 5(2)) and had not ensured that the level of protection was not undermined (Art. 44). She issued two reprimands and an order to ensure any continued transfer rests on the new EU-US Data Privacy Framework or an Article 46 safeguard, and to report within one month. No fine was imposed, given the new adequacy decision and the circumstances. The controller had argued that it does not transfer any data to third countries.

A complaint lodged in Austria by an Austrian resident, represented by noyb, concerned a Politis news website that allegedly embedded Facebook tools which passed visitors' IP addresses and cookie data to Facebook Inc. in the United States after the Schrems II ruling invalidated the EU-US Privacy Shield. The publisher did not answer the Commissioner's repeated written questions. The Commissioner found breaches of the accountability principle (Article 5(2)) and of the transfer rules (Article 44). She issued a reprimand for each and ordered the publisher, if it keeps using the tool, to ensure transfers rest on the new EU-US Data Privacy Framework or an Article 46 safeguard and to report within one month. She decided that no administrative fine was justified.

ELTA, the Greek postal operator, notified the authority of a ransomware attack in March 2022 that encrypted systems and led to personal data being leaked on the dark web. The authority investigated and found that ELTA had not kept adequate technical and organisational security measures, breaching the integrity and confidentiality principle and the security of processing obligation. It treated these as two separate infringements of high gravity affecting 4–5 million people. Taking into account aggravating and mitigating factors and ELTA's turnover, it imposed a fine of EUR 2,995,140, equal to 1% of the last annual turnover.

A law firm, acting for a former customer of Brivio Limited, complained that the company did not answer a right-of-access request under Article 15 GDPR within one month. The company said a staff error caused the delay and that it had been receiving a high volume of similar requests from the same firm, which it argued were manifestly unfounded. The Commissioner rejected those arguments, found an infringement of Article 12(3) GDPR, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000.

The Greek DPA examined forty complaints together about unsolicited promotional calls made for the energy company Elpedison by its call-centre partners (Befon, Call Experts, Teleraise, Zitatel, PLEGMA NET). Some calls reached subscribers listed in the opt-out register, others followed failures to apply objections or delays in loading the register. The Authority found that Elpedison did not adequately supervise its call-centre processors (Article 32 GDPR) and fined it EUR 127,709. It also ordered Elpedison to design a call-centre audit procedure within six months, and issued a warning for six calls that breached Article 11 of Law 3471/2006. Fines were also imposed on Call Experts (EUR 10,000), Zitatel (EUR 6,000 and EUR 5,000) and PLEGMA NET (EUR 20,000).

The Information Commissioner issued an enforcement notice to the Home Office over its GPS electronic tagging pilot for asylum claimants on immigration bail. The Commissioner found that the Home Office failed to carry out a data protection impact assessment meeting Article 35(7) before the pilot started, and failed to demonstrate compliance with the principles of lawfulness, fairness, transparency and data minimisation as required by Article 5(2). The notice requires the Home Office to provide updated documents within 28 days. No fine was imposed.

The Croatian DPA checked a company's website on its own initiative using the EDPS Website Evidence Collector and found that cookies, including analytics and marketing cookies, were set on first page load without informed consent. The cookie banner and privacy notice also did not give adequate information on legal basis, cookie types, purposes and retention. The Agency found breaches of Articles 6(1)(a), 7, 5(1)(a) and 13(1)-(2) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 20,000, about 0.1% of the maximum possible fine, and ordered proof of payment. The company had introduced a new consent banner (Cookiebot in November 2022, Didomi in May 2023) during the proceedings.
The DPA reprimanded a controller for failing to honor the data subject's right to object to receiving payment reminders, even though the data subject consistently made timely payments.

The DPA confirmed that telecommunication service providers have to provide access to location data they process under national data retention legislation contrary to the controller who argued that such legislation provided a full exemption for the right to access.

The complainant asked an association to erase his data so that it would stop sending him letters, but it kept writing to him after his request of 27 July 2023. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision suspecting breaches of Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 17(1) GDPR. It ordered the association to comply with the erasure request. This is not a merits decision, and the association may ask for a merits hearing within 30 days.

A complainant, represented by a French e-reputation company, complained to the Belgian DPA after a search engine refused three requests to delist a 2007 newspaper article about him. The Litigation Chamber found that the company is a commercial company, not a non-profit body, and so the complainant was not validly represented under Article 80(1) GDPR as read with Belgian law. Because the complaint was not validly brought, the Chamber closed the case on technical grounds without ruling on the merits of the delisting request. The decision notes that this does not prevent the complainant from filing a valid complaint later.

A report to the Garante complained that the public transport company TPER used a season-ticket application form where consent to customer surveys/marketing and to service SMS looked mandatory and was not specific, with only a signature at the bottom. After investigating, the Garante found unlawful processing: invalid consent, deficient and unclear information notice, excessive 10-year retention, and failure to update documents by 25 May 2018 (accountability). It fined the company EUR 50,000, ordered a ban on using data collected on invalid consents for marketing and service communications, deletion of that data, and delivery of the new privacy notice to data subjects. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

An employee complained that the Chamber of Commerce published on its online notice board a board resolution naming him, concerning an employment lawsuit he had brought against it. The name was shown in clear for a few days, then replaced with 'omissis', but the court, case number and judgment details still allowed him to be identified. The Garante found the dissemination had no legal basis and breached the lawfulness principle. It fined the Chamber EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on its website. No further corrective measures were needed because the publication had ended.

A customer of the CoopVoce mobile service objected to promotional processing and asked for access to and erasure of his data, but the company did not properly handle the requests and kept sending promotional SMS. The Garante also inspected the company in April 2023 and found issues with consent wording for marketing, and with five-year retention of images collected at events and on social media. It found violations of the storage limitation principle, the 30-day deadline for replying to requests, the right of access, the right to object to marketing, and Article 130 of the Code. It ordered the company to change its marketing consent wording, and fined it EUR 90,000, with publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA received two complaints and two breach notifications about the South Tyrol health authority's corporate electronic health record (dossier sanitario), which health staff not involved in the patients' care had repeatedly accessed. The cases were merged. The Garante found the processing unlawful for breaching the basic principles, security and privacy-by-design rules, and special-category data rules. It imposed three fines of EUR 25,000 each, totalling EUR 75,000, and ordered publication. No corrective measures were imposed because the authority had started disciplinary proceedings and adapted its systems.

Sigma s.r.l., a Vodafone dealer with two shops in Trento province, was investigated by the Guardia di finanza. Its owners and staff activated SIM cards and services in customers' names without their knowledge and charged them for phones never delivered, using customer data and ID documents. The Garante found breaches of lawfulness, fairness, accountability, legal basis, data protection by design and information duties. It fined the company EUR 150,000, banned further processing of this kind, and ordered publication of the decision. The company filed no defence.

A data subject, represented by NOYB, complained that a website's cookie banner had no button to reject all cookies, so consent was not valid. The Chambre Contentieuse found that the banner had been changed before the complaint was forwarded to it, so the only alleged violation was no longer founded, and that the banner also met the EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce guidance. It dismissed the complaint on opportunity grounds, without a decision on the merits and without a fine.

A complainant, represented by NOYB, alleged that a website's cookie banner made withdrawing consent harder than giving it, with no clearly visible withdrawal option. The Belgian Chambre Contentieuse dismissed the complaint on opportunity grounds, without examining the merits. It noted that by the time of the referral the website had a cookie banner with a reject-all button and a footer link to cookie settings, so the complaint's object had disappeared. It also observed that non-essential cookie categories were not pre-ticked and that the banner matched the EDPB Cookie Banner Taskforce report. No fine or order was imposed.

A former employee complained that her photo, which she had not consented to, was still published on her ex-employer's website and social media in a recruitment campaign. She asked for its removal on 31 August 2023, and the employer replied the same day that it followed its work rules. In a prima facie decision (not a decision on the merits), the Litigation Chamber found that no legal basis under Article 6 seemed to apply, so the publication was probably unlawful. It found a possible infringement of Article 17(1)(d) GDPR and ordered the employer to comply with the erasure request within 30 days, while the employer could ask for a merits hearing.

The DPA held that a municipality’s unsolicited disclosure of the data subject’s identity to a property owner was unlawful. The data subject had reported the property owner for supposedly blocking a sidewalk to the municipality.

A data subject asked a first aid training provider for access to his data but was required to return a signed request form and a copy of his identity card by email, and the provider could not say why it could not identify him from the details he gave. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that requiring an ID copy as a standard practice breached the data minimisation principle and Article 12(6), and that the practice was not a means under Article 12(2) to facilitate rights. The provider also kept the data longer than its own retention period, which breached Articles 5(1)(e) and 25(2). The decision ordered the provider to change its practice, to comply with the access request, to send the data to the data subject, and to delete outdated customer data; no fine was imposed.

A former employee complained that his employer used the GPS tracking system of a company car he had been given to locate him while he was on annual leave, outside working hours, after he did not answer work calls. The Authority found unlawful processing of his location data and incomplete information about the tracking system. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 for the unlawful processing and a reprimand for the transparency breaches. The Authority examined the case in its session of 10 January 2024; the decision document is dated 16 February 2024.

An employee complained that his employer's company had used GPS location data from a company car he had been given, to show he used the vehicle outside working hours, and that he had not been properly informed about this tracking. The Authority found that the company recorded the vehicle's location data outside working hours, although it had only allowed use of the car during working hours, and that the information given to the employee was not individual, complete and clear enough to be certified. No fine was imposed. The company received a warning to adapt its information on the vehicle tracking system, and an order to make that information individual, complete, clear and certifiable.
The ICO issued an Enforcement Notice and 100,000 GBP fine against a controller due to unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals who were on the 'do not call' list.
The DPA reprimanded Bolt for failing to enable the rectification of a data subject’s phone number. However, the controller implemented the respective possibility in the course of the procedure.

The complainant made an access request after a credit application was refused. The controller sent him the content of its own file, but only identity and contact details of the controllers of two other credit files it had consulted, and it did not clearly confirm that he had received all his personal data. The complainant also said the controller held an image of his identity card, which was not provided. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision finding a possible infringement of Article 15 GDPR and ordering the controller to comply with the access request, including a copy of the data, within 30 days. This is not a decision on the merits, and the controller can ask for a merits hearing.

The DPA fined a controller that was processing employees’ fingerprint data € 360,000 because it failed to disclose processing and storage information to data subjects, lacked security measures ensuring the data’s confidentiality and failed to carry out a data protection impact assessment.

A complainant asked a Belgian politician several times from 2018 onward to erase his name, address and photo, which the politician had published on his personal website. The Litigation Chamber had already ordered erasure in Decision 16/2021, but the data stayed online until after a hearing was scheduled in late 2023. The Chamber found violations of GDPR Articles 12(3), 12(4), 17(1) and 31 and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000.

An employee of the company, without authority, copied CCTV footage from the security control centre and sent it to a data subject via WhatsApp and uploaded it to Telegram. The company said it had deleted the footage and ended the employment, and the inspectorate found its security measures compliant with Article 25(1). On its own initiative, the inspectorate then examined the audio recording built into the CCTV system and found that it breached Article 5(1)(a) and (c) and Article 6(1), because it records conversations beyond what the Interior Ministry's rules require and without a legal basis. It ordered the company to stop audio recording with video surveillance and report on compliance by 12 March 2024. No fine was imposed.

UniCredit notified the Garante of a cyberattack on its mobile banking portal in October 2018, in which customer identifiers and personal data were accessed. The Garante found that the portal leaked personal data in HTML responses even after failed logins and lacked effective protection against bot-driven brute-force attacks, which breached the integrity and confidentiality principle and the security obligations. It declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 2,800,000, with no corrective order. The Milan court later rejected the bank's opposition and confirmed the decision.
The DPA fined a processor €800,000 for engaging a sub-processor without the prior authorization of the controller and for the belated notification of a data breach to the controller.

Medtronic Italia notified a data breach: a team member emailed users of the MiniMed Mobile diabetes app with all addresses visible in the 'To' field instead of 'Bcc'. About 5,001 addresses were exposed worldwide, 732 of them in Italy. Because the emails reveal that recipients use a diabetes app, the Garante treated this as disclosure of health data. In the same proceeding it found that the company's privacy information for the Health Partner Share feature, which links a patient's account to a doctor's account, left out the legal basis for sharing data with healthcare professionals. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 9, 12, 13 and 32 and imposed a total fine of EUR 300,000, of which EUR 250,000 is for the email breach. It ordered no corrective measures because the conduct had ended and the company had changed its procedures and its privacy notice. It also ordered publication of the decision.

A customer complained to the Garante that a partnership never answered his access request under Article 15 GDPR, filed on 3 July 2020. The partnership blamed an administrative error and pandemic-related organisational difficulties. The Garante found that it had not replied within the Article 12(3) deadline and that its later reply only listed data types without giving the actual data. It ordered the partnership to answer the access request within 30 days and imposed a fine of EUR 5,000.

A complainant's health-related document (a refusal of travel and stay benefits for out-of-region treatment) was emailed by an administrative employee of the Sassari local health authority to a wrong third-party address. The authority also failed to answer the Garante's request for information until proceedings were opened. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5, 9 and 32 GDPR and Article 157 of the Italian Code. It fined the authority EUR 18,000, considering the severity low (one data subject, unintentional), and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ceased.

The Garante fined Enel Energia S.p.A. EUR 79,107,101 after finding that its sales-agency platform N.Eve let shared or unauthorised users load telemarketing contracts, obtained from illegally acquired contact lists, into Enel's systems from 2015 to 2022. The Garante found weak security measures (credentials could be used simultaneously by several people, and access-log alerts were switched off), insufficient control of agencies and sub-agents, and a flawed Art. 28 contract framework. It also ordered Enel to notify the affected data subjects, adopt technical measures, and report back within 30 days, and it ordered publication of the decision.

A data subject asked the controller, which runs the adult website mydirtyhobby.de, to erase his account and data by email in June and July 2020, but received no completed erasure and his account stayed active. The controller said it had replied with deletion options and a verification link to its ManageMyData platform, which the complainant never completed. The Cypriot Commissioner found breaches of Articles 12(4), 13 and 17 GDPR: the controller did not tell the data subject it would not act on the request, the platform gave no information about the controller, and the erasure was not carried out. She issued a reprimand for Articles 12(4) and 13, a EUR 1,500 fine for Article 17, and orders to erase the data and to fix the platform information and the request-handling procedure.

An employee of a regional waste management agency complained that her 2019 evaluation form was registered in the agency's protocol system in a way visible to all authorised users, and that she had no contact with the data protection officer (DPO). The Garante found no unauthorised access, but found that the agency designated its DPO about three years late, did not publish the DPO's contact details, and did not notify them to the authority. Because these violations came from a single conduct, one fine of EUR 6,000 was imposed, with publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased.

Following ten complaints brought by noyb in August 2021 and an inspection on 1-2 August 2022, the Garante examined the cookie banners on Maggioli's websites. It found that on eight sites the banner did not explain what the 'X' button meant, that the short notice wrongly cited legitimate interest and a right to object for cookies, and that Maggioli had chosen a processor (OneTrust) whose banner did not comply. Taking into account Maggioli's prompt fixes, its cooperation, the absence of intent and of harm, and the change of provider, the Garante decided not to impose a fine and issued a reprimand (warning) under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR.

The complainant asked the controller to erase his email address, which it used for unsolicited marketing. After an earlier decision (09/2023) ordered erasure, he still received marketing emails, because the controller held a second account under a different email address that had not been covered by the first request. Once the controller identified that account, it erased that address too. The Litigation Chamber accepted this explanation, found no new infringement of Articles 12(3) and 12(4) read with Article 17(1) GDPR, and dismissed the complaint.

A school employee complained that medical and other documents were missing from her personnel file, and that her former supervisor (called Y1 in the decision) had taken the file and possibly copied it. The Litigation Chamber dismissed the complaint without a finding of infringement. The complaint against the supervisor was dismissed on technical grounds because it lacked evidence of a GDPR breach. The complaint against the file controller (called Y2 in the decision) was dismissed on policy grounds because no evidence was shown and the complainant had shown no significant personal impact. The Market Court rejected the complainant's appeal on 9 October 2024.

The Romanian DPA investigated Account Exchange SRL after a complaint that it had used the personal data of several individuals to open virtual-currency current accounts in their names. It found that the company processed the names of individuals from an administrative-territorial unit, in order to send notices about accounts opened in their name, without consent or any other legal basis. It also found that the company did not supply all the information and documents the authority requested. The company was fined RON 9,940.40 (about EUR 2,000) for the failure to provide information, and received a warning for the breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6 GDPR.

Iberdrola, acting as data processor for other group companies, ran a customer database in which logical separation between companies was inadequately configured, so an attacker using one company's application could access other companies' customer data and exfiltrate it. The AEPD found a loss of confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(f)) and deficient security measures (Art. 32) and rejected Iberdrola's arguments on non bis in idem, equality and proportionality. It imposed two fines: EUR 2,000,000 for Art. 5(1)(f) and EUR 1,000,000 for Art. 32, totalling EUR 3,000,000. The decision ends administrative remedies; reposición or appeal to the Audiencia Nacional is possible.

Energya VM Gestión de Energía, S.L., (“Energya VM” or “data controller”) entered into a contractual relationship with Nivalco, to promote its services. Nivalco contacted individuals from its database, offering discounts or insurance purportedly from their current energy supplier. However, these offers were actually agreements with Energya VM. Many data subjects only discovered they had entered into agreements with a new company when they noticed unexpected charges on their bank accounts. AEPD's investigation began following police reports of alleged crimes by energy supply companies. Energya VM failed to conduct a prior risk analysis analysis,ensure GDPR compliance in processing, and adopt measures for GDPR-compliant sales pitches. The AEPD found Energya VM negligent for allowing Nivalco’s deceptive practices to persist despite being aware of them at some point during the contractual relationship and imposed fines.
The Belgian DPA issued a warning against a controller for failing to provide clear information under Article 13 to the data subject.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in January 2024 into an owners' association in Miercurea Ciuc after a complaint. The association had posted a member's notification, with her name and home address, in the association's WhatsApp group, which was unlawful and excessive disclosure. It also gave no proof of replying to her access, erasure and objection request, and did not show it had carried out corrective measures ordered in an earlier report. It was fined a total of 2,486.2 lei (about EUR 500) and ordered to take corrective measures.

The Spanish DPA examined a personal data breach at the electricity distributor I-DE, in which a cybercriminal exfiltrated customer data through a vulnerable web application with weak password policy and access from suspicious IPs. It found a breach of confidentiality (Art. 5(1)(f)) and inadequate security measures (Art. 32), rejecting I-DE's argument that this violated the non bis in idem principle. It imposed two fines: EUR 2,500,000 for Art. 5(1)(f) and EUR 1,000,000 for Art. 32, totalling EUR 3,500,000. The mitigating factor was the quick reaction to the attack, while the aggravating factors were negligence and the large-scale, continuous processing of data of about 21 million customers.

The Latvian data protection authority reviewed a complaint by the photography company AQUAPHOTO against its first-instance fine of EUR 1,000 (decision of 15 December 2023). AQUAPHOTO took photographs of visitors at a water park and treated those photos on the basis of coloured wristbands and implied consent, while visitors were not properly informed or given a real choice. The authority found that the consent was not valid and that the transparency and information duties were breached, and it did not find a breach concerning the biometric data. The director dismissed the complaint and left the EUR 1,000 fine in place.

The CNIL restricted formation fined a company that runs a French website for peer-to-peer property listings and services. Following online and on-site inspections in 2022, the CNIL found that the company kept user account data for far longer than necessary, lacked adequate information for data subjects, had no compliant Article 28 contract with its processor, and had weak security (including plain-text storage of passwords). The company was fined EUR 100,000 for breaches of Articles 5(1)(e), 13, 28 and 32 GDPR, and the decision is to be published, without naming the company after two years.

Following an on-site inspection in September 2021, the CNIL examined a loyalty-programme company that phoned prospects from data files bought from data brokers who collected them through online prize-draw forms. The company could not say which legal basis it relied on. The restricted committee found that neither legitimate interest nor consent was valid, because the forms did not let people reasonably expect calls from the company and did not secure proper consent. The alleged Article 32 breach was not upheld. It imposed a EUR 310,000 fine for breach of Article 6 GDPR and ordered publication, with the company no longer named after two years.

A complainant who began registering with Airbnb in May 2019 and then asked for erasure of his data was asked to send a copy of his ID, which he refused. The DPC, as lead authority under Article 60, found that the request for an ID copy was not a valid Article 6 legal basis for the erasure request and that requiring the ID constituted an infringement of the data minimisation principle under Article 5(1)(c). The DPC found no infringement regarding the ID request at account creation or regarding transparency under Article 13, and issued a reprimand rather than a fine, noting Airbnb had discontinued the practice.

This text is not the decision itself but a CNIL web page listing all sanctions by the restricted committee. The entry dated 31 January 2024 concerns a dental surgeon dealt with under the simplified procedure. The listed failings are a lack of data security and failure to respect the right of access to health data. The listed outcome is an administrative fine of EUR 5,000. No reasoning, reference number or calculation is given.

The text is not the decision itself but the CNIL's public table of sanctions. On 31/01/2024 the table has six entries. Only one carries a EUR 10,000 fine: a business-support company, handled under the simplified procedure, for a data security failure. The table gives no reasoning, articles, calculation or reference number.

This is not the decision but the CNIL's overview table of sanctions. Its 31 January 2024 row for a website editor publishing technology news (simplified procedure) lists a failure to ensure data security. The sanction listed is an administrative fine of EUR 20,000. The table gives no reasoning, no articles and no reference number. Another 31 January 2024 row, for a property-ad website editor with a EUR 100,000 fine, is a different decision and was not used.

Datatilsynet, the Danish data protection authority, decided in the Google Workspace for Education (Chromebook) case against 53 Danish municipalities, represented by KL. It accepted that the municipalities may disclose pupils' data to Google for the original purposes of delivering and securing the service. It found no adequate legal basis in the Folkeskole Act for disclosure to Google for the derived purposes, such as developing Google's products and measuring performance. It issued an order (påbud) to bring the processing into line with the GDPR by 1 August 2024, with no fine.

The DPA found that a public institution violated security measure obligations when it stored a document with employees' personal data, including names and use of sick leave, in an intranet folder that was accessible to unintended recipients.

The Latvian Data State Inspectorate reviewed the website grosauto.lv, run by SIA GZ AUTO, on 19 January 2024. It found that the cookie banner accepted cookies without a real choice, that analytics cookies ran before any consent, and that marketing cookies were set once a visitor clicked accept, with no working option to refuse analytics or marketing cookies. It found the processing did not comply with GDPR Article 5(1)(a), Article 6(1) and Article 7. Instead of a fine, it ordered the company to fix the consent mechanism so cookie use complies with GDPR and the national e-privacy rules, and to report by 1 March 2024.

As part of the EDPB's 2023 coordinated action on the designation and position of data protection officers, the Greek authority sent a questionnaire to 31 public bodies, including the Ministry of Rural Development and Food. The Ministry did not answer the questionnaire or a reminder, and it was found to have had no DPO from 4 August 2022 to 20 June 2023 because the previous contract expired and was not renewed for lack of funds. The authority found infringements of Article 31 (cooperation with the supervisory authority) and Article 37 (DPO designation). It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 for Article 31 and EUR 20,000 for Article 37, EUR 25,000 in total.

As part of the EDPB's 2023 coordinated action on the designation and position of the DPO, the Greek authority sent a questionnaire to 31 public bodies, including the Municipality of Athens. The Municipality did not answer by the deadline, nor after a reminder and phone calls, and only submitted it on 18 December 2023 after being summoned to the Plenary. Its claim of technical problems with the survey link was rejected because the link was working. The Authority found a breach of Article 31 GDPR (cooperation with the supervisory authority) and imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000.

A government office included ‘nonbinary’ as a response in a form question about sex. The DPA held that the response constituted processing of a special category of data and violated the principle of data minimization.

The Hellenic DPA imposed €1,000 administrative fine on an accountant for unlawfully collecting and using personal data without proper authorisation, violating Article 5(1)(a) GDPR and Article 6(1)) GDPR.

During the Covid-19 emergency a municipality published on its Facebook page a map showing the homes of people with coronavirus or in quarantine, and several ASL documents with insufficiently redacted names, addresses, phone numbers and diagnoses. The municipality also ignored the Garante's two information requests and notified its data protection officer's contact details only late. The Garante found unlawful processing without a legal basis, a breach of the ban on disseminating health data, and breaches of Art. 157 of the Code and Art. 37(7) GDPR. It fined the municipality EUR 3,000, 2,000 and 1,000 (total EUR 6,000), ordered it to stop the dissemination and report back, and ordered publication of the decision.

In October 2022 the Garante had ordered the municipality to give a data subject free copies of CCTV footage and to report back within 30 days. The municipality did not report by the deadline and only delivered the footage on 14 February 2023, about 69 days late, and fully informed the Garante on 15 February 2023, about 70 days late. The Garante found a breach of Article 58(2)(c) GDPR and Article 157 of the Code, in connection with Article 58(1)(a). It treated the conduct as intentional and of high gravity, but took account of the municipality's small size, no previous violations and its action after the notice. It fined the municipality EUR 8,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

A teacher complained that the school published on its website about thirty-seven managerial determinations about staff absences and substitute teachers in the 2021/2022 school year, which exposed her and other staff to absences being recorded online. The school said the publication was an error by administrative staff, that it covered four staff members and disclosed only names and dates of absence, and that it removed the documents after the complaint and changed its templates. The Garante found that publishing the data online had no valid legal basis and breached the principles of lawfulness and minimisation, and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 plus publication of the decision on its website.

This is not the decision itself but the CNIL's overview page of sanctions. The row dated 24 January 2024 concerns a pharmaceutical wholesale business dealt with under the simplified procedure. The listed shortcomings are data security, lack of cooperation with the CNIL, the record of processing activities, and the use of processors offering sufficient guarantees recruited with the controller's authorisation. The outcome shown is an administrative fine of EUR 20,000. No reasoning, articles or calculation are given in the text.

The DPA issued a favorable opinion after a prior consultation with a company using AI for throat cancer organ preservation research. However, at least three attempts to contact unreachable patients in the study is considered a proportionate effort.

A paediatric hospital notified a personal data breach caused by a bug in the DNLAB laboratory software supplied by Dedalus Italia, its processor. Lab reports were linked to the wrong patients, so 6 patients' reports were seen by unauthorised people and 8 patients could not access theirs. The Garante found that Dedalus failed to provide adequate security measures and periodic testing, and unlawfully disclosed health data. It fined Dedalus EUR 8,000 for the breaches of Articles 5(1)(f), 9 and 32, and ordered publication of the decision.

A former professional collaborator complained that the company did not respond to his requests to object, restrict processing and erase his work email account after the collaboration ended. The company had redirected the account's mail to another company mailbox for at least seven months and gave no reply to the formal rights request. The Garante found breaches of data minimisation and of the rules on erasure and replying to data subjects, and fined the company EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

Two former employees complained to the Garante that their former employer kept using company logbooks showing their names after they left, kept their email account active for about seven months after termination, and did not provide training certificates. The Garante found the company unlawful for continuing to use the logbooks after an erasure request and for not answering an access request. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 12, 15 and 17 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 (EUR 1,000 per conduct). It also ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website, and archived one part of the complaints.

A daughter asked a healthcare provider for access to her late father's medical records. The provider refused, relying on a written authorisation in which the father had forbidden giving his data to her. She challenged the refusal before the Information Commissioner under the Patients' Rights Act, saying her father had dementia when he signed it. The Commissioner set the refusal aside and sent the case back to the provider, which has to decide again within 30 days, because the provider had not established whether the father was able to understand what he was prohibiting.

The Catalan DPA fined a controller €3000 for violating the principle of confidentiality when it sent emails to numerous family members of patients at an occupational health center without using the blind copy option.
The DPA imposed a € 200,000 fine on a controller that granted a third party a duplicate SIM card without the data subject’s consent and without verifying the third party’s identity.

The Belgian DPA found the controller to have breached Article 15 GDPR in conjunction with Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR for having replied to the complainant's access request after the one-month deadline.

The CNIL's published list of restricted-committee sanctions has a row dated 22 January 2024 for an attorney under the simplified procedure. The listed breach is insufficient cooperation with the CNIL, and the administrative fine is EUR 500. The list gives no further detail, and the underlying deliberation is not in the text.

A student complained that a lecturer at the University of Iceland electronically monitored his use of the Canvas learning platform and used peer assessment from classmates in grading. The Data Protection Authority found that checking his Canvas activity was not electronic monitoring under the Act, and that the university could rely on the public-interest basis for this processing. However, the student had not been adequately informed about the lecturer's possibilities to review his activity or about the use of peer assessment, so the processing breached the transparency requirement and the university failed its information duty. The operative part finds the processing non-compliant with the Act and the GDPR on fair and transparent processing and the information duty. No fine or order is stated.

The DPA fined a videogame company €90,000 for its use of forum moderators without proper data minimisation or security measures limiting their access to personal data. The controller paid a reduced fine of €72,000 in accordance with national law.

A sole trader running a business sent an e-mail with an unencrypted database attachment listing the participants of a conference to an unauthorised recipient in August 2021. The database included contact details, employers, job titles, payment status, vaccination status (health data) and, for three people, PESEL numbers. The controller did not notify the UODO of the breach and did not properly notify the affected persons. The UODO found infringements of Article 33(1) and Article 34(1) and (2) GDPR, imposed an administrative fine of PLN 9,903.60, and ordered notification of the three persons whose PESEL numbers were exposed.

The Belgian DPA's Litigation Chamber fined the data broker Black Tiger Belgium (formerly Bisnode Belgium) a total of EUR 174,640 through three separate fines. The company processed personal data on a large scale, relying on legitimate interest, without proactively and individually informing the people concerned, and kept the data for 15 years. It also failed to answer the complainants' access requests fully and its record of processing activities was incomplete. Besides the fines, the Chamber ordered corrective measures, including a halt to the B2B Data Quality service until data subjects are notified, and a permanent ban on processing data of people for whom no contact details exist.

The Romanian data protection authority completed an investigation in December 2023 into TECHNINK LEB SRL after the company notified a personal data breach. Customer data was accessible on the company's website, exposing a significant number of clients. The authority found that appropriate technical and organisational security measures were not in place and fined the company RON 14,904.30 (stated as EUR 3,000). It also ordered a regular testing plan and password complexity procedures.

The text is not the decision itself but the CNIL's overview table of sanctions from its restricted committee. The entry dated 15/01/2024 concerns a lawyer handled under the simplified procedure. It lists failure to cooperate with the CNIL and failure to respect the right to erasure, with an administrative fine of EUR 5,000. No reasoning, articles or reference number are given in this table.

The Romanian DPA concluded an investigation into Alior Bank's Bucharest branch, carried out in cooperation with the Polish authority after a former client complained. The client had asked for deletion of his data and had his accounts closed, yet the bank kept sending unsolicited e-mails and SMS messages, and earlier sent commercial e-mails despite an objection. The bank's centralised system in Poland kept monitoring former clients and messaging them after contracts ended, which the authority found to be processing for an incompatible purpose. It fined the bank 84,491.7 lei (about EUR 17,000) and ordered regular monitoring of compliance with Articles 5 and 6 GDPR, including reporting any needed system reconfiguration to the Polish head office.

The Italian DPA ran checks on public bodies' notification of their data protection officer (DPO) contact details and found the Municipality of Siracusa had never notified them, despite a 2020 reminder. The failure covered two successive DPOs (2018 and 2022). The municipality only notified the current DPO on 5 June 2023. The Garante found a breach of Article 37(7) GDPR, imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

The Italian DPA checked the website of the Libero Consorzio comunale di Caltanissetta and found that it had published its DPO's contact details but had not communicated them to the Authority. The Consortium argued staff shortages and the effects of the covid period. The Garante found a violation of Article 37(7) GDPR and fined the Consortium EUR 2,000, taking into account that it had remedied the omission on 30 May 2023, had no previous violations and that the breach was negligent. The decision is to be published on the Garante's website.

During a check of the Province of Catanzaro's website, the Italian DPA found that the Province had published its data protection officer's contact details but had never communicated them to the Authority. The Province said it had done so on 27 April and pointed to staff shortages caused by financial crisis and the pandemic. The Garante found these explanations insufficient to close the case and declared the processing unlawful for breach of Article 37(7) GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 2,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

The Italian DPA checked the website of the Province of Sassari and found that it had published its data protection officer's contact details but had never notified them to the Authority. The Province said it was probably an IT mishap and notified the details after being alerted. The Garante found a breach of Article 37(7) GDPR and fined the Province EUR 2,000, also ordering publication of the decision on its website.

The Italian DPA learned from press reports that the Municipality of Trento, with a research foundation, was testing AI systems (Marvel, Protector, Precrisis) using public-space cameras, microphones and social media data. After an investigation it found unlawful processing: breaches of fairness and transparency, no legal basis (including for special category and criminal-offence data), missing information to data subjects, unlawful disclosure to third parties and a deficient impact assessment. It fined the municipality EUR 50,000, banned further processing of the data collected and ordered its deletion, and ordered publication of the decision. Charges on Article 28 and on police access to Twitter network data were dropped.

A patient complained that an aesthetic medicine centre run by David S.r.l. posted on its public Instagram profile a video of him during a non-surgical rhinoplasty procedure. The company relied on a signed consent form and said the patient was not identifiable and that no health data was shown. The Garante found the processing unlawful: no valid legal basis, health data was disseminated contrary to the Italian Code ban, and the information notice was deficient. It fined the company EUR 8,000, ordered it to rewrite its information notice within 90 days, and ordered publication of the decision.

A doctor left medical prescriptions for patients in an unattended metal box outside his practice, accessible to anyone, mostly not in sealed envelopes; 67 prescriptions were found during checks in Feb-April 2023. The doctor claimed patients had consented and that the practice was occasional, and said he had removed the box, but filed no defence after the proceedings were opened. The Garante found violations of Articles 5, 9 and 32 GDPR and Article 2-septies(8) of the Italian Code, and fined him EUR 20,000, with publication of the decision.

The Garante investigated the company running the PIGNA portal, which lets banks and notaries exchange mortgage documents, after the National Council of Notaries asked for clarification. It found that the company sent notaries summary reports on open files on its own initiative, outside the banks' instructions, so it was acting as a controller. It did so without a valid legal basis and without proper information to the notaries. It also wrongly relied on legitimate interest, not contract, for notaries' registration and credentials. The late privacy notice had already been fixed. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, fined the company EUR 5,000, ordered it to bring the reporting processing into line within six months, and ordered publication.

The complainant asked a recruitment agency several times in August and September 2023 to erase her data and stop calling and emailing her. The agency confirmed on 5 September 2023 that her data had been removed, but she was called again on 15 September 2023. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision under Article 95 WOG. It found that the agency potentially breached Articles 12(3), 12(4) and 17(1) GDPR, and ordered it to comply with the erasure request within 30 days and report back. No fine was imposed, and this is not a decision on the merits.

IMY, as lead supervisory authority for a complaint transferred from Germany, examined Klarna Bank AB's handling of the complainant's request of 8 June 2020 to correct the e-mail address linked to a Klarna card. Klarna said the address could not be changed on an issued card, so the complainant had to order a new card, which would affect the complainant's creditworthiness. IMY found that Klarna breached Article 16 (failure to rectify) and Article 12(2) (failure to facilitate the exercise of the right to rectification). Because the infringements were minor, IMY issued a reprimand instead of a fine.

A data subject complained that the controller had not answered his access request (sent 31 August 2023) within one month and had kept and used his data for marketing SMS. The Slovenian Information Commissioner found that, when the complaint was lodged on 16 October 2023, the controller had not yet decided the access request, which breached Article 15 in conjunction with Article 12 GDPR and Article 14 ZVOP-2. The controller had answered on 18 October 2023, and the Commissioner found no unlawful retention under Article 6 because the data had already been deleted. No fine or order was imposed, and the marketing-SMS complaint was referred to the telecoms regulator AKOS.
The Spanish DPA decided that Law 25/2007 did not release the controller from its obligation to give access to geolocation data in the case of an access request.

A former contractor complained that the controller had not deleted his professional mailbox and email address after his contract ended on 6 June 2023, and had not answered his access request of 16 October 2023. The Litigation Chamber issued a prima facie decision, not a decision on the merits. It warned the controller that keeping the mailbox active after the end of the working relationship appears to breach Article 5(1)(b), (c) and (e) and Article 5(1)(a) read with Article 6(1). It also ordered the controller to comply with the access request within 30 days and to report back. The controller may request a hearing on the merits within 30 days.

The Austrian DSB issued an administrative penalty decision (Straferkenntnis) against a football association that ran a publicly searchable database of league players on its website. The association had no suitable technical and organisational measures to fully delete player data when erasure was required (Art. 25(1) GDPR, from 25 May 2018), it did not fully comply with an erasure request made on 23 September 2020 (Art. 17(1) GDPR), and it did not follow a supervisory authority order (Art. 58(2)(c) GDPR). The DSB imposed a fine of EUR 11,000 at the bottom of the statutory range, after the proceedings had been suspended pending the CJEU ruling of 5 December 2023 on fines against legal persons. The decision is stated to be final.

The DPA ordered a retail company to stop using on-site security cameras to monitor employees. The company had based this practice on its legitimate interests without considering the fundamental rights of the employees.

This is a mid-year press release from the Hamburg data protection authority summarising fines of EUR 130,000 imposed up to July 2024 across 14 proceedings. For this record, a hotel was fined EUR 16,000 because it collected and stored identity card data without a legal basis. The other fines in the release (advertising company, support ticket systems, logistics firm, online retailer, police officers, private individuals) relate to other cases.

This is a mid-year press release from the Hamburg data protection authority, dated 22 August 2024. It reports fines totalling EUR 130,000 across 14 administrative offence proceedings up to July 2024. One of them was a EUR 6,000 fine on an online retailer for reporting a data breach very late. The release also lists fines on an advertising company, a hotel, a logistics company, two firms with support-ticket systems, police officers and private individuals.

This is a mid-year summary press release from the Hamburg data protection authority, not a single decision. It reports that the authority imposed fines totalling EUR 130,000 up to July 2024 in 14 administrative offence proceedings. One passage says two fines were imposed on members of the police for running database queries for private purposes. No amount, article or date is given for these two fines. The other fines in the release (advertising company, hotel, logistics firm, online shop, private persons) are separate cases.

This is a mid-year press release by the Hamburg data protection authority summarising 14 fine proceedings up to July 2024, totalling EUR 130,000. It is not a single decision. The part matching Fino's entry is a EUR 11,500 fine on a company in the advertising industry for breaching deletion obligations, whose IT system also had technical security gaps. Other fines in the release concern a hotel, support-ticket systems, a logistics firm, an online retailer, police officers and private persons.

This is an interim press release from the Hamburg data protection authority summarising fines imposed up to July 2024, totalling EUR 130,000 across 14 administrative offence proceedings. It covers many different cases, not a single decision. The one matching Fino's record is a logistics company that paid EUR 32,000 for improperly disposing of delivery-driver lists. No articles, reasoning or calculation for that fine are given.

This is the 2024 annual report of the Saxon data protection commissioner. In the section on administrative offence proceedings in the non-public sector, the authority says it issued fine notices of EUR 120,000 and EUR 22,080 against two companies for serious breaches of the duty to cooperate with the supervisory authority (Art. 31 GDPR). Both companies had ignored requests for information and documents for a long time and were not swayed by coercive penalty payments. In one case the information came only after more than two years and four months and five coercive penalties; in the other after more than a year and four coercive penalties. The report names neither company and gives no day for the decisions.

The annual report of the Saxon data protection commissioner for 2024 says that, for the first time, she conducted fine proceedings directly against legal persons. For serious breaches of the duty to cooperate with the supervisory authority (Art. 31 GDPR) she issued fine notices against two companies, of EUR 120,000 and EUR 22,080. Both companies had ignored requests for information and documents for a long time and were not moved even by coercive penalty payments. In one case the information came only after more than two years and four months and five coercive penalty payments; in the other after more than a year and four coercive penalty payments. The report does not say which delay belongs to which amount. The report does not name the companies.

This is the Berlin data protection authority's 2024 annual report, not a single decision. Section A.II.1 describes one fine of EUR 60,000 against a provider of a practice management platform and patient portal for security gaps. Patients could view practice email credentials and the registration data of other patients, and a faulty end-to-end encryption allowed a downgrade attack affecting 198 institutions and 1,623,732 patients. The authority applied the EDPB fining guidelines. It counted health data at risk against the provider, and counted cooperation, immediate shutdown of the systems, a catalogue of measures and prompt notification of those affected in its favour.

The Berlin data protection authority's 2024 annual report says a large share of its fine proceedings again concerned police officers who looked up personal data of third parties in the police database POLIKS for non-official purposes, and in some cases reused it. In 2024 it opened 50 proceedings against police officers and issued 23 fine notices. Example cases include an officer who ran 170 queries on his ex-girlfriend and her relatives, and an officer who did his own investigations on a theft he had suffered. The report gives no amount, no articles and no names for these fines. The report-wide total (all fines, not only police) is 25 fine notices with 164 fines.

The Hessian data protection commissioner's 2024 annual report describes two proceedings against doctors' practices that published patient data in replies to Google reviews. The doctors addressed reviewers by their real names even though the reviews were pseudonymous, and in other cases disclosed treatment details, diagnoses and medication beyond what the patients had written. The commissioner found this breached the lawfulness principle (Art. 5(1)(a) with Art. 6(1) and Art. 9(1) GDPR). In one case a fine of EUR 3,700 was imposed, and in the other EUR 3,300. Both decisions are final.

The annual report describes two proceedings against doctors' practices for publishing patient data in replies to Google reviews. The commissioner found that the practices had processed health data unlawfully, in breach of the lawfulness principle read with Arts. 6(1) and 9(1) GDPR. In one case the fine was EUR 3,700, and in the other a fine notice of EUR 3,300 was issued. Both decisions became final. The commissioner treated the public disclosure of extensive health information and the intentional conduct as aggravating. Full admission, cooperation and prompt deletion of the comments counted in the doctors' favour.

The commissioner's 2024 annual report describes a case in which a doctor's practice manager kept patient files in open shelves in an unlocked home office, so unauthorised third parties could access them. He also had a partner photograph outgoing invoices from the patient records and send them over WhatsApp. The commissioner found breaches of the confidentiality principle (Art. 5(1)(f) with Art. 32) and of the lawfulness principle (Art. 5(1)(a) with Art. 9(1) and 6(1)). He fined the practice owner EUR 2,500. Mitigating factors were negligence and the measures taken afterwards (lockable cabinets, a safe, renewed training). Aggravating factors were the scope of the processing and the sensitivity of the health data.

The 53rd annual report of the Hesse data protection commissioner describes a fine against a freelance website operator whose site had no privacy notice. The authority formally ordered the operator to provide detailed privacy information and threatened a EUR 2,000 coercive penalty. The operator ignored the final order, and two further coercive penalties of EUR 2,000 each were set and collected, yet the operator still did not comply. The authority then imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 on top of the EUR 6,000 in coercive penalties. The fine notice has become final. The report names neither the operator nor the date of the decision.

This is the Hessian DPA's 53rd annual report, not a single decision. In its fines chapter it describes a settlement procedure against a large financial company. Complaints showed late replies to access requests, sensitive customer documents sent to wrong recipients and telemarketing calls without consent. The company admitted the violations and cooperated, so the DPA discontinued proceedings on two violations and applied a fine reduction. Fines totalling EUR 496,000 were imposed and the notice became final.

The text is the 53rd annual report of the Hessian data protection commissioner, not a single decision. It describes many fine cases from 2024. The case matching Fino's entry concerns an IT company that sent advertising e-mails to over 2,700 people in a one-off campaign, including the complainant, who was never a customer and had not signed up. The processing had no valid consent and could not rest on legitimate interests because the unsolicited e-mail advertising rules were not met. The commissioner fined the company EUR 10,000, taking into account that it was a first offence, little data was involved, there was negligence and cooperation.

The 2025 annual report of the Berlin data protection authority describes several fines against health-sector employees who misused patient or staff data for private purposes. One of them is a fine imposed 'last year' (so in 2024) on a receptionist at a psychiatric outpatient clinic. After several failed attempts to make contact, he used a female patient's email address to tell her he wanted to get to know her better at a meeting. The report gives no amount, no legal articles and no reasoning for this particular fine.

The annual report of the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern data protection authority describes a fine against an unnamed hospital. An anonymous complaint said that an unlocked cabinet of patient files stood in a freely accessible construction area. An on-site inspection found over 100 old patient files that should long have been destroyed. The hospital reacted at once, had the files recovered and destroyed, and promised better retention and destruction processes. A fine is the rule in such cases, but the hospital's special circumstances and its immediate cooperation clearly reduced it. The report gives no amount and cites no articles.

The Saxon data protection commissioner's 2025 annual report describes an administrative offence case against a police officer. The officer had filed criminal complaints and supervisory complaints against several colleagues and, over many months, systematically monitored and documented their work. In doing so he took photos of police documents without authorisation and viewed his colleagues' working-time records, as well as those of uninvolved third parties. A fine notice was issued in 2024 and, after a long procedure, the local court confirmed it in 2025 while reducing the amount. The report does not state the amount of the fine.

The Thuringian data protection authority's annual report for 2024 describes a case in which a wildlife camera was used to film and secretly record sound at a cemetery. The authority found the processing unlawful: visitors expect a high degree of privacy there, and neither a legitimate interest nor justifying necessity applied. A fine under Art. 83(5) GDPR for breaching Arts. 5, 6, 7 and 9 was imposed on the camera operator and became final. The report gives no amount for this fine. No further measures were needed because the operator had already removed the camera before the fine proceedings began.

The French DPA fined NS Cards France, an electronic money distributor, €105,000 for keeping personal data longer than necessary, having incomplete privacy policies, failing to sufficiently secure personal data, and failing to seek user consent regarding not strictly necessary cookies.

Following 27 complaints, the CNIL carried out online inspections in October 2020 and June 2021 of a company's web domain and its email service. It found that cookies were placed on users' devices in France, including by about fifteen advertising companies, without valid consent. The CNIL held that it was competent, since the one-stop-shop does not apply to cookie operations under the ePrivacy rules and the French company counted as an establishment. It fined the company EUR 10,000,000 for breaching Article 82 of the French Data Protection Act and ordered the decision published, with the company no longer named after two years.

The CNIL restricted committee fined a French company that collects prospect data through online contest forms and sells that data to advertising partners. The company relied on consent, but its forms bundled participation in a contest with agreement to pass data to partners, so the consent was not valid and the transmission had no legal basis (Article 6). It also had no adequate record of processing activities (Article 30). The committee imposed a EUR 75,000 fine, ordered compliant consent forms under a EUR 1,000 per day penalty, and ordered publication. On 20 May 2026 the Conseil d'Etat reduced the fine to EUR 50,000.

The Hellenic DPA accepted the complaint in which the data subject complained about Google's refusal to delete search results that appeared based on her name. The data subject claimed that because of the results of the search engine for several years she was unable to find a job, while she added that keeping them has a negative effect on her professional carrer.

The CNIL's restricted committee fined the French warehouse logistics company EUR 32 million for breaches of GDPR Articles 5(1)(c), 6, 12, 13 and 32. The breaches concerned real-time scanner-based monitoring of warehouse employees' productivity, quality and idle time, and the failure to inform temporary workers properly. The decision also ordered publication, without naming the company after two years. According to the header, the Conseil d'État later reduced the fine to EUR 15 million, finding that the real-time indicators did not breach Article 6(1)(f). The published decision no longer names the company; the name comes from the Conseil d'État judgment of 23 December 2025.

A student complained that an email sent from the adult education institute's information system to its course enrolees advertised a third party's sports courses with prices. The email was sent by a part-time teacher, against the institute's instructions and unrelated to its activities, to promote her own summer teaching for another employer. The Deputy Data Protection Ombudsman found that the institute, as controller, had breached the principles of lawfulness and purpose limitation in Article 5(1)(a) and (b) and the accountability duty in Article 5(2), because using students' email addresses for this purpose was equivalent to disclosing them without a legal basis. No fine was imposed; the institute received a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b).

The DPA held that it is unlawful to use data that was collected for marketing purposes to assess the creditworthiness of data subjects as this further processing violates the principle of purpose limitation under Article 5(1)(b) GDPR.

The Polish data protection authority handled a complaint about the processing and disclosure of a person's data by a company. The company did not answer the authority's requests for explanations, nor the notice that fine proceedings had been opened, nor the request for its financial data. The authority opened its own proceedings and found a breach of the duty to cooperate (Art. 31) and of the duty to give access to information (Art. 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR). It treated the breach as intentional and imposed a fine of PLN 18,864, about EUR 4,000. The decision is marked as final.

The Italian DPA examined a video surveillance system operated by a sole trader at a butcher's shop, found by the municipal police during an inspection on 10 June 2022. The system was running but no information sign about the cameras was displayed. The controller did not respond to the notice of proceedings. The Garante declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR, imposed a fine of EUR 2,000, ordered compliance by posting informative signs, and ordered publication of the decision.

A voter agent (umboðsmaður) of a political party complained that agents were required to carry an ID badge showing the party they represented during the 2022 Kópavogs elections. Persónuvernd found the processing lawful: it had a legal basis in the electoral law, the complainant was informed when he was asked for a photo, and the party affiliation was already public. The processing was found to comply with the GDPR and the Icelandic data protection act, and no infringement was found.

A card loyalty programme operator (Y) suffered a data breach in August 2019 at its processor, affecting up to 89,429 people in 27 EU member states. The Litigation Chamber held that the referral to the Inspection Service was lawful and that the breach was notified to the authority in line with Article 33 GDPR. It found no repeated breaches showing systematic failings under Articles 24 and 32 GDPR, and, given the rapid response and the measures taken, concluded that the controller committed no GDPR infringement. No fine or order was imposed, and the decision is published without the parties' identifying details.

The Polish data protection authority opened proceedings of its own motion against the Minister of Health after data on a doctor's prescription (health data) was taken from the national electronic health platform and published on the social network X. It found unlawful processing of special category data, failure to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures (WhatsApp was also used to pass on data), and failure to give the doctor the full information required on the breach. It fined the Minister PLN 100,000, the maximum for public finance sector bodies, and ordered security measures and notification of the data subject.

The Hungarian DPA found three joint controllers to have breached Article 6(1)(a) GDPR, Article 9(1) GDPR, as well as Article 12 and 13 GDPR for having unlawfully contacted a data subject after the latter had signed up to support a political movement.

A Polish consulate sent court correspondence for the Kraków District Court in a divorce case. The postal operator delivered it damaged and incomplete, and the Minister of Foreign Affairs notified the UODO of the breach. The court did not report the breach to the UODO or inform the people concerned, arguing that the UODO has no supervisory power over its judicial activity. The UODO found breaches of Articles 33(1),(3) and 34(1),(2) GDPR and imposed a fine of PLN 10,000. It also ordered the court to notify the four affected people (the parties and their two children) within 3 days, and discontinued the remainder of the proceedings.

The Dutch DPA investigated International Card Services (ICS), a credit and debit card issuer, after consumer signals and complaints about its re-identification of customers online from 2019 (the ID&V process). It found that ICS did not carry out a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) before introducing this large-scale processing, which was likely to pose a high risk. ICS's internal risk process and its parent bank's earlier analysis were held not to be equivalent to a DPIA. The AP fined ICS EUR 150,000 for breaching Article 35(1) GDPR, using the base amount of the policy category II and treating the seriousness as low.

The Austrian DPA decided complaints by two complainants against the OSCE and four of its staff about the handling of data from a work phone during an internal investigation. It dismissed the complaint against the four staff members on the merits and rejected the complaint against the OSCE itself, because the organisation is immune from the DPA's action under the host-state agreement. No fine or order was imposed.

A data subject complained that the City of Reykjavík had not given her a full copy of the personal data it held from her occupational licence applications (1998 to 2023), and that the security of that data was inadequate. The city had provided the data it could find, but some documents, including medical and criminal-record certificates, could not be located. The Authority found the access request was handled lawfully, given that the right of access covers only data that exists. However, because sensitive health data was lost while in the city's custody, the city had not ensured adequate security, which breached the security principle and Article 32 GDPR. No fine was imposed.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in November 2023 into a controller who is a private individual. The investigation started after a report. The individual had not carried out a corrective measure the Authority had set in an earlier minutes (procès-verbal) and had not allowed the Authority access to the personal data and information it needed for its inspection. The Authority found a breach of Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR and fined the individual 993.84 lei, equal to 200 euro.
The Icelandic DPA ordered a controller to remove a post from a social media platform which constituted processing in violation of Article 6(1)(f) GDPR.

The ICO fined the UK Ministry of Defence £350,000 for disclosing personal information of people seeking relocation to the UK after the Taliban took control of Afghanistan. In September 2021, the MoD's Afghan Relocations and Assistance Policy team sent group emails using the 'To' field, exposing email addresses and in some cases thumbnail photos and a location, for 265 unique addresses in total. The ICO found the MoD lacked appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent such disclosures. The fine was reduced from a £1,000,000 starting point, first for remedial action and then under the ICO's public sector approach.

The Polish DPA had ordered a company, in two final decisions of November and December 2022, to erase the personal data of two individuals who had complained. The company never collected the decisions or reminders, and never showed that it had complied. The DPA opened its own proceedings and fined the company PLN 23,580 (about EUR 5,000) under Article 83(6) GDPR for not complying with the corrective orders. The company, which the DPA treated as small-scale but profitable, did not provide its financial data or cooperate.

The DPA warned the City Tourist Board that while publishing photos of public events on public squares is lawful, publishing a specific photo of the applicant's minor daughter lacked legal basis and purpose under Articles 5 and 6 GDPR.
The French DPA fined a municipality €5,000 for failing to designate a DPO and to cooperate with the DPA, therefore violating Article 31 GDPR and Article 37(1)(a) GDPR.

The Austrian DSB fined a limited company for breaking the breach-notification rules. The company had known of a security breach since 6 March 2023 but reported it to the DSB by email only on 24 April 2023, late, and limited the report to general information because it only wanted to satisfy its insurer. It then did not give the fuller report the DSB asked for twice (24 and 26 April 2023), a failure to cooperate under Art. 31 GDPR. The DSB imposed one fine of EUR 5,900 under Art. 83(4)(a) GDPR for both breaches. The decision is final.

The Austrian data protection authority fined a bank for breaching a data subject's right of access. After an access request of 23 January 2023, the bank treated it internally as a deletion request, deleted the data, and gave only general information. The authority found a breach of Article 12 in conjunction with Article 15(1) GDPR, committed through negligence, and imposed a fine of EUR 9,500. The decision is final.

ANSPDCP finished an investigation of Veranda Obor S.A., which runs a shopping centre, after a report of a possible GDPR breach. The company had published on its website the names and email addresses of a significant number of people who took part in a prize draw organised by the centre. The authority found that it had not put in place appropriate technical and organisational security measures, leading to unauthorised disclosure of or access to the data. It fined the company RON 14,823.60 (equivalent to EUR 3,000) for breaching Article 32(1)(b) and 32(2) GDPR.

The Dutch DPA found that Uber breached the GDPR transparency rules towards its drivers. The guidance notes were offered only in English, and the response to an access request was not in an easily accessible form. The access/portability form was hard to reach in the driver app. The privacy statement was not specific enough on retention periods and on transfers, and it did not mention the right to data portability. The case began with complaints that a French NGO filed with the CNIL on behalf of 172 drivers, and the CNIL passed them to the AP. The AP imposed a joint administrative fine of EUR 10,000,000 on Uber B.V. and Uber Technologies Inc.

The Austrian DSB fined a restaurant company that ran a video surveillance system at its take-away premises, recording the interior, including the kitchen and pick-up workstations of its staff, around the clock and keeping the footage for 14 days, with no legal basis under Art. 6(1) GDPR. The DSB found breaches of Art. 5(1)(a) and (c) and Art. 6(1), and a second breach: the company kept no record of processing activities, as Art. 30(1) requires. It imposed one fine of EUR 20,000, at the bottom of the available range, plus EUR 2,000 in costs. The company's turnover could not be established, so the DSB estimated it into the lowest band. The decision is final.

The Austrian DSB issued a penal decision (Straferkenntnis) against a housing company for not cooperating in a complaint procedure. The authority had asked for a statement three times (17 November 2021, 11 April 2022 and 3 June 2022), each time citing the duty to cooperate under Art. 31 GDPR and the possibility of penal proceedings. The company's data protection officer said the requests had been lost in internal forwarding, but the DSB found at least conditional intent. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000, at the low end of the Art. 83(4) range, and the decision is stated to be final.

The Romanian DPA completed an investigation into Hora Credit IFN SA after a complaint that the company emailed the complainant documents containing another client's personal data and kept sending messages after being told of the error. It found inadequate security, failure to notify the breach to the authority within 72 hours, and no proof of a reply to the complainant's access request about the source of his data. Three fines totalling EUR 24,000 (RON 119,296.8) were imposed, together with corrective measures requiring better security, training, an internal breach policy, informing the affected client and answering the complainant.

An employee complained that his employer, Sirio S.p.A., passed his personal data (residence address and personal mobile number) to a bank so that a deposit card could be issued in his name, without giving him a privacy notice or having a valid legal basis. The Garante found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a), 6 and 13 GDPR. It imposed a fine of EUR 1,000 and ordered the company to draft a compliant privacy notice and report to the Authority within 60 days.
