A health trust in north Milan notified a personal data breach: a nurse employed there obtained a printout of her husband's Covid test result from a colleague, without any delegation, and the husband later complained. The Garante found that, since March 2020, the trust had configured its health dossier so that all nurses and hospital doctors could access all patients' data across all wards, regardless of involvement in care. It found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and (f), 9, 25 and 32 GDPR. It ordered the trust to restrict dossier access to staff involved in care and to introduce anomaly alerts within 90 days, and fined it EUR 40,000, with publication of the decision.

A company notified UODO of a personal data breach (an employee disclosed staff and client data to a third party). UODO asked it twice for explanations in the breach case, but the company never answered. UODO opened separate proceedings of its own motion and found a breach of the duty to cooperate with the authority and to give it access to information. It fined the company PLN 11,790 (about EUR 2,500), treating the intentional, long-lasting non-cooperation as aggravating and the company's small scale as a reason for a modest fine.

The local police inspected a kebab shop run by a sole proprietorship and found a working video surveillance system with no signs informing people about the cameras. The Garante opened sanction proceedings and found the processing unlawful for breaching the transparency principle and the duty to give information under Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR. The business did not cooperate or show it had complied. The Garante fined it EUR 2,000, ordered it to report on measures taken within 30 days, and ordered publication of the decision.
The DPA fined a doctor €1,500 for unauthorized access to a data subject’s medical records and for failing to explain her legal basis.

The DPA fined UK Ministry of Defence €409,080 (GBP 350,000) for disclosure of 265 unique email addresses of individuals seeking relocation from Afghanistan following the Taliban's ascent to power in the summer of 2021.

The DPA held a violation of the Regulation and its Protection of Natural Persons Against Data Processing of a Personal Character and the Free Circulation of this Data Law of 2018, Law 125(I)/2018, by the Examinations Service of Directorate of Higher Education of the Ministry of Education, Sports and Youth in relation to Statistical Processing Methods of the scores of the candidates who took part in the 2019 Written Examinations for Registration and Ranking in the Appointment Tables.

A job applicant for an emergency responder post at Neyðarlínan (the Icelandic emergency call centre) complained that the National Commissioner of Police (RLS) looked her up in its police case register (LÖKE) at Neyðarlínan's request and passed the information on. The Authority accepted that the check could be justified by a task carried out in the public interest, but found that RLS could not show she had been properly informed about the vetting or what it involved. The processing therefore breached the fairness, transparency and information requirements. No fine or order was imposed.

The Finnish DPA ordered a healthcare provider to reliably identify persons in its electronic healthcare appointment booking system. In its decision, the DPA stated that requesting a name and personal identity code is not enough to verify a person's identity.

The Belgian DPA proposed a settlement between the data subject and Mediafin, a Belgian media group, concerning the setting of cookies on the website of the Belgian newspaper De Tijd. Inter alia, Mediafin should ensure that the withdrawal of consent in the cookie banner should not take more clicks than granting consent.
The Belgian DPA proposed a settlement to a controller asking them to modify their cookie banner in order to comply with Article 4(11), 6(1)(a) and 7 GDPR.
The DPA found that Radio Télévision Belge de la Communauté Française did not use misleading cookie banners on their website.

A data subject complained that Techno Security s.r.l. had not answered his access request of 29/02/2020, made after the company installed a security system at his home. The company did not reply until 14/11/2020, only after the complaint and the Garante's inquiry had started, which was almost nine months after the deadline. The company also did not cooperate in the proceedings. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12(3) and 15 GDPR and imposed a fine of EUR 1,000, and it ordered publication of the decision on its website.

A complaint reported that a gym operated by Spartan Gym S.S.D. a r.l. in Rome had four video cameras without information signs and without the safeguards required by Article 4 of Law 300/1970. A Guardia di finanza inspection in July 2022 confirmed the cameras, the missing signs and the missing extended privacy notice, and that no Labour Inspectorate authorisation had been requested. The company later put up signs and applied for authorisation, but the Garante still found breaches of Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Codice, and imposed a fine of EUR 3,000 with an order to pay and publication of the decision.

Limit Call, a call centre selling electricity contracts by telephone, bought contact lists from a list provider in Moldova and called about 32,000 people without checking consent, privacy notices or the opposition register. After an earlier complaint and a EUR 10,000 fine for not replying to the Garante, the authority inspected the company in May 2023. It found missing information notices, no proven consent, no register check, a dead email address for data subject requests and insufficient cooperation. The Garante banned the unlawful processing, ordered deletion of the data and corrective measures, and fined the company EUR 60,000.

The Hungarian DPA reprimanded a controller for breaching Article 6(1)(f) GDPR. Although the surveillance system installed by the controller was legitimate, it covered a too wide area and, thus, the processing at the time of the complaint was not proportionate.

The controller, a Slovenian Ministry, was found to have infringed Article 15 GDPR in conjunction with Articles 12 and 14 of the Slovenian Data Protection Act since, at the time of the data subject's complaint with the Slovenian DPA, it did not fully comply with the complainant’s access request.

Persónuvernd audited how Reykjanesbær's primary schools used Google Workspace for Education for pupil records, as part of an EDPB-coordinated review of cloud services in schools. It found several breaches, including weak processor arrangements with Google, unclear purposes, storage and minimisation failures, a late and inadequate DPIA, and unsafe transfers to the United States before 10 June 2023. It ordered the processing brought into line with the law by 29 February 2024 and imposed a fine of ISK 2,500,000. The fine part was later withdrawn by a decision of 19 March 2026 in case 2025122459.

The Icelandic Data Protection Authority audited how Reykjavík's primary schools used Google Workspace for Education for about 8,500 pupils in 2021-2022. It found several breaches by the City: it had not met its accountability duties when choosing Google as processor, the Google processing agreement did not meet all legal requirements, pupil data were processed for incompatible purposes, data minimisation and data protection by design were not met, the DPIA was inadequate, and transfers of data to the USA lacked safeguards. The Authority ordered the processing brought into line with the law and imposed a fine of ISK 2,000,000. The note at the top of the text says the fine part was annulled by a decision of 19 March 2026.

The Icelandic DPA audited how Garðabær municipality's primary schools used Google Workspace for Education, a cloud service for pupils' data. It found several breaches by the municipality, including an inadequate processor contract with Google, purpose and storage problems, a deficient DPIA, and unsafe transfers of pupils' data to the United States. It ordered the processing brought into line with the law and imposed a fine of ISK 2,500,000. A later decision of 19 March 2026 in case 2025122461 withdrew the fine part.

The Icelandic DPA audited the City of Hafnarfjörður's use of Google Workspace for Education in its primary schools. It found several GDPR breaches, including inadequate processor controls, unclear purposes, missing or late data protection impact assessment, weak data minimisation and storage limits, and no secure transfer safeguards for data sent to the United States. The DPA ordered the processing brought into compliance by 29 February 2024 and imposed an administrative fine of ISK 2,800,000. Per the note at the top, the fine part was withdrawn by a decision of 19 March 2026.

Persónuvernd audited the City of Kópavogur's use of Google Workspace for Education in its primary schools and found multiple GDPR breaches. The city was found to have failed its accountability duties, to have a processor contract with Google that did not meet all requirements, to have unclear and incompatible purposes, to have no DPIA, to have neglected storage limitation, data minimisation and data protection by design, and to have transferred data to the US without safeguards until the EU-US adequacy decision of 10 June 2023. It was ordered to bring the processing into line with the law and fined ISK 3,000,000. The text published with the decision says the fine part was later withdrawn (19 March 2026, case 2025122457).

The Belgian DPA issued a preliminary decision in which it ordered the controller to comply with a request of the complainant to delete data used for direct marketing communication, following the complainant's objection request pursuant to Article 21 GDPR.

The Danish Data Protection Agency examined Aarhus University Hospital's publication of photos of patients, with health information, on its Instagram account. It found that consent could not serve as the legal basis, because of the unequal relationship between patients and a public hospital, and that the processing breached the principles of Article 5(1). It issued a reprimand to Region Midtjylland and ordered it to delete posts containing patients' health information within four weeks. No fine was imposed.

After an on-site inspection of NAV on 6 September 2023, the Norwegian DPA found that NAV's governance system and the confidentiality protection in its case-handling IT systems were inadequate, identifying 12 violations. On 27 November 2023 it sent a notice of intended decision proposing orders to fix the failings and an administrative fine of NOK 20 million. The fine was driven by long-term broad access to special-category data about many people and by intent, including ignoring earlier orders. This is only a preliminary notice; NAV could comment, and the final decision and amount were to be set later.

The DPA fined a controller for several infringements in handling the data of minors and parents: no proper and documented legal basis, information was confusing, partly untrue and not properly given, data were retained after consent was withdrawn.

An anonymous complainant alleged that cameras in the six shops of the controller were placed so that staff were under permanent surveillance by the security company, contrary to the purpose of security and CBA No. 68. The Litigation Chamber held that camera surveillance for security and theft protection is allowed, but must not subject staff permanently to monitoring of their work, which breaches the data minimisation principle in Article 5(1)(c) GDPR. Because the decision is a prima facie decision under Article 95 WOG, it issued a warning and a recommendation rather than a fine, noting the company is relatively small. The controller may ask for a merits hearing within 30 days.

A customer of Alpha Bank, acting for his partnership that fell victim to online fraud, requested access to CCTV footage of his branch visit and to web banking log files. The bank supplied the logs late and could not provide the footage because it had been deleted after its 45-day retention period had expired, before the request was handled. The Authority found that the bank breached the access right and the response deadline (Arts 15(1),(3) and 12(3)), and breached the lawfulness principle by deleting the data after the request. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000.
The Cypriot DPA imposed a fine in the amount of €45,000 on the Open University of Cyprus for failing to put in place appropriate security measures according to Article 32 GDPR.

The Romanian DPA completed an investigation into Libra Internet Bank SA after a complaint about how the bank answered a data subject's access request, following a corrective measure the authority had earlier imposed. The bank did not fully comply with that measure: it did not give the complainant all the information on categories of data, purposes and recipients, within the deadline, and it showed no proof of sending a completing reply. The authority found a breach of Articles 58(2) and 83(5)(e) and (6) GDPR and fined the bank RON 7,454.25 (about EUR 1,500). It also ordered the bank to send the full reply to the complainant by post.

The Danish DPA issued a negative opinion regarding the City of Copenhagen’s plan to develop AI tools to identify citizens in need of rehabilitation, as the national law relied upon for the purposes of Article 6(1)(e) GDPR and Article 6(3) GDPR was not specific enough in relation to the scope of the AI’s use.

The Polish DPA fined the partnership W. sp. j. PLN 14,148 (stated as about EUR 3,000) for failing to give the authority the information and access it requested under Art. 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR. The requests arose from a data subject's complaint about marketing use of her data. The company did not collect the registered letters sent to its seat, did not answer, and did not respond to the penalty proceeding or e-mail reminders. Because it did not provide its 2022 financial data, the authority estimated its size and set the fine at about 0.015% of the statutory maximum. The decision is marked as final (prawomocna).

Fifty employees of Autostrade per l'Italia complained that the company never answered their access requests about the data used to calculate their severance pay (TFR) and related information. The company argued that the data were at issue in pending labour court cases and relied on a restriction of rights, and that employees could see their payslips on an internal platform. The Garante found that the company gave no proper reply to the access requests, breaching Articles 12 and 15 GDPR. It ordered the company to satisfy the requests within 60 days and fined it EUR 100,000, and ordered publication of the decision.

A former employee of Amazon Italia Transport complained that his access request under Article 15 GDPR, sent by certified email in September 2021, went unanswered within the legal deadline. The company replied only on 4 February 2022, after the Garante opened its inquiry, almost six months late. It also did not ask the person to narrow the broad request nor inform him of any extension and the reasons. The Garante found breaches of Articles 12 and 15 and imposed a fine of EUR 40,000, with publication of the decision.

A mother complained that psychiatric expert reports about her deceased son, including health and criminal-investigation data, were visible online. The reports came from training material of a medical course organised by Cluster S.r.l., which uploaded them to its management system and emailed a link to 26 participants. The link was reachable on the web without any authentication. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5 and 32 GDPR and fined Cluster EUR 18,000, also ordering publication of the decision. It saw no need for corrective measures because the link had been removed. It treated the earlier emailing of the link as time-barred, but the security failure as continuing until the investigation.

A local police officer from another municipality complained about the municipality of Castel Goffredo. Its local police station had a video camera with audio recording facing the front office, and the recording of a conversation between the complainant and a colleague was handed to the other municipality's police command, where it was used against the complainant. After the complainant died, the Garante continued the case on its own initiative. It found that the camera was installed without the labour-law safeguards (union agreement or authorisation), that the audio was recorded without a legal basis, that there was no proper information notice and no DPIA, that the recording was kept beyond the set retention period, and that the data were disclosed without a legal basis. It imposed two fines, EUR 30,000 and EUR 20,000, totalling EUR 50,000, and ordered the decision to be published. No further corrective measures were ordered because the camera had already been removed.

A newspaper published an article about a robbery at a woman's home, including her name, a photo taken from her Facebook profile, the street and a photo of the building, details from a neighbour's interview, and information about her minor daughter's school. The complainant objected, and the publisher removed the online version during the proceedings, but the print version remained in the archive. The Garante found that the publication breached the principle of minimisation and the essentiality of information for journalism, and it issued a reprimand. It also ordered a ban on further processing of the complainant's and her daughter's identifying data, except for mere storage for possible court use and limited research access to the print copy.

A woman whose appearance in an old TV clip was repeatedly rebroadcast by the programme Striscia la notizia asked the broadcaster RTI to erase her personal data by certified email (PEC) sent to its registered address. RTI did not respond, and the content stayed online until after the complaint. The Garante found the publication compatible with journalism rules, but held that RTI should have answered the erasure request under Article 12, since the PEC was a valid official channel. Because the content had already been removed, it issued a warning (avvertimento) rather than a fine.

A lawyer sent a certified email (PEC) notifying a court attachment to the business email address of a company in which the complainant is a partner. The email was addressed to the complainant by name, and the company's staff could access the mailbox. The Garante found that the lawyer had no valid legal basis for the disclosure and had breached the data minimisation principle. It imposed a fine of EUR 500 and did not order corrective measures, because the conduct had already run its course.
In the context of a procedure under Article 60 GDPR, the Irish DPC reprimanded Microsoft Operations Ireland Limited for violations of Article 12(4) GDPR and Article 17 GDPR.
